title: In, At and On: Places, Events and Transport
summary: Choose natural place prepositions for everyday institutions, events, buildings, towns and transport. Contrast at as a place or event, in as an interior or geographical area, and on/in for different means of transport.
learningObjectives: Describe where people are using established expressions such as in bed, at work and at university.
Select at for attendance at an event or a visit to someone’s home and in when describing an interior.
Distinguish in a city from at a station or stop on a journey.
Use on with buses, trains, planes, bicycles and similar transport, but in with cars and taxis.

explanation.heading: Institutions and everyday activities
explanation.body: Some place expressions follow established patterns rather than a rule about physical containment. We say in bed, in prison and, in British English, in hospital for someone receiving care. We say at home, at work, at school, at university and at college when referring to a normal activity or situation. Home can also appear without at after be: She is home. With activities, say study at home or eat at home.
explanation.example: The designer is at work, but her brother is still in bed.

explanation.heading: At events and social occasions
explanation.body: Use at for participation in an organised activity: at a lecture, at a ceremony, at a workshop, at a meeting or at a wedding. At names the event as an occasion rather than telling us the precise room a person occupies. We also usually say at someone’s house, or at someone’s when house is understood.
explanation.example: We met an old neighbour at a community meeting.

explanation.heading: At versus in with buildings
explanation.body: Both at and in can sometimes describe someone being at a building, but the focus differs. At can mark a venue or the place where an event takes place; in can identify its interior. We can meet at a hotel, while a narrow staircase is in the hotel. For stations and airports, at is the usual broad location expression.
explanation.example: The exhibition was held at the gallery, and a sculpture stood in the entrance hall.

explanation.heading: In towns; at stops along a route
explanation.body: Cities, towns and villages are geographical areas, so we normally say in Bristol, in a small town and in that village. When a city name is used as a station or stopping point on a route, at can refer to that point: a coach can stop at York. The difference is between living within an area and stopping at a named point.
explanation.example: My cousin lives in York, but this express train does not stop at York.

explanation.heading: On public transport; in cars and taxis
explanation.body: We normally say on a bus, on a train, on a plane and on a ship for passengers travelling aboard them. We say in a car and in a taxi for people inside those vehicles. The conventional patterns also include on a bicycle, on a motorbike and on a horse. These collocations are more useful than a rule based solely on size.
explanation.example: The group took the train, while their guide travelled in a taxi.

explanation.heading: British and American usage
explanation.body: Some expressions vary by variety of English. For a patient, British English often uses in hospital, whereas American English usually uses in the hospital. Both refer to receiving treatment; the difference is a regional article pattern, not a change from in to at. The exercises in this unit use the British English institutional expressions from the reference.
explanation.example: In British English, you might say that a patient is in hospital for a few days.

comparisons.title: Attending an event versus being inside the venue

left.label: At: occasion
left.example: I spoke to her at the science fair.
left.note: At identifies the event where the conversation happened.

right.label: In: interior
right.example: I found a quiet corner in the exhibition hall.
right.note: In focuses on the physical space inside the building.

comparisons.title: A city as an area versus a route stop

right.label: At: journey point
right.example: The coach stops at Oxford before going north.
right.note: At treats Oxford as a stop on the route.

left.label: On: train or bus
left.example: We met on the early train.
left.note: Passengers travelling aboard a train use on.

right.label: In: car or taxi
right.note: Passengers inside a taxi use in.

comparisons.title: Activity or institution versus physical space

left.label: At work: normal activity
left.example: My sister is at work this afternoon.
left.note: At work describes her situation as working.

right.label: In a room: interior
right.example: My sister is in the staff kitchen.
right.note: In specifies the enclosed room where she is.

examples.sentence: My grandfather stayed in hospital for three nights.
examples.note: In hospital is a conventional British English phrase for a patient receiving treatment.

examples.sentence: The organisers welcomed visitors at the careers fair.
examples.note: At indicates participation at an organised event.

examples.sentence: A guide is waiting at the airport to meet the arriving guests.
examples.note: At identifies the airport as a meeting location.

examples.sentence: There are two emergency exits in the theatre building.
examples.note: In focuses on what is inside the building.

examples.sentence: Our relatives have lived in Glasgow for many years.
examples.note: In is normal for residence within a city.

examples.sentence: She read her notes on the train and answered a call in the taxi.
examples.note: On the train and in the taxi follow the conventional transport patterns.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We travelled to the airport on a taxi.
commonMistakes.correct: We travelled to the airport in a taxi.
commonMistakes.why: Passengers ride in a taxi, not on a taxi.
Use in for a city regarded as an area where people live.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I will study on home this evening.
commonMistakes.correct: I will study at home this evening.
commonMistakes.why: A home activity takes at home; on home is not an English place expression.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We met our friends in a wedding last week.
commonMistakes.correct: We met our friends at a wedding last week.
commonMistakes.why: Use at to identify the social event where you met them.

studyTips: Build small groups of complete phrases: at home / at a conference / at the airport; in bed / in a town / in a taxi; on a train / on a bicycle.
Test the focus of a building sentence: does it identify a venue (at) or a detail inside it (in)?
Practise describing the same journey in three ways: in the city, at the station, and on the train.

exercises.prompt: The visitors were all ___ the international research conference yesterday.
exercises.feedback: At a conference identifies attendance at the organised event.

exercises.prompt: Please call me when you are waiting ___ the airport entrance, beside the taxi sign.
exercises.feedback: At the airport entrance identifies a specific meeting or waiting point.

exercises.prompt: The passengers found it difficult to stand ___ the crowded bus.
exercises.feedback: We normally say passengers travel on a bus; at and under do not describe being aboard it.

exercises.prompt: Their new apartment is ___ a village near the coast, not in a large city.
exercises.feedback: A village is a geographical area, so use in a village.

exercises.prompt: After the appointment, Leah went to visit her aunt ___ . (her aunt’s house; write the conventional at-expression)
exercises.feedback: At someone’s house is the standard way to identify a visit location.

exercises.prompt: The children are ___ while their parents prepare breakfast. (resting under the covers; write the two-word place expression)
exercises.feedback: Someone resting or sleeping under the covers is in bed.

exercises.prompt: I saw the announcement ___ . (a meeting yesterday; write at plus the event)
exercises.feedback: An organised meeting is treated as an event: at a meeting.

exercises.prompt: The engineers travelled ___ . (a taxi; write the conventional in-expression)
exercises.feedback: Passengers travel in a taxi, not on one.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the incorrect location preposition in this sentence: Our cousins live at Birmingham, where they have a small bookshop.
acceptedAnswers: Our cousins live in Birmingham, where they have a small bookshop.
exercises.feedback: Use in when describing residence in a city.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the incorrect location preposition in this sentence: I met the author on a literary festival last month.
acceptedAnswers: I met the author at a literary festival last month.
exercises.feedback: At identifies the event where the meeting happened.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the incorrect location preposition in this sentence: We travelled to the station on a taxi after the concert.
acceptedAnswers: We travelled to the station in a taxi after the concert.
exercises.feedback: Use in with a taxi when talking about its passengers.

exercises.prompt: Correct only the incorrect location preposition in this sentence: I plan to work on home tomorrow because the office is closed.
acceptedAnswers: I plan to work at home tomorrow because the office is closed.
exercises.feedback: The normal activity expression is work at home.

speakingExercises.prompt: A colleague asks where Ellen is during her normal working day. Given fact: Ellen / be / at work. Say one sentence beginning “Ellen”.
speakingExercises.feedback: At work describes Ellen’s usual working situation.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your brother is still asleep under the covers. Make one sentence starting with “My brother” and using “in bed”.
speakingExercises.feedback: In bed is the usual expression for someone resting or sleeping.

speakingExercises.prompt: Report where you met Sofia. Facts: I / meet Sofia / at a conference / yesterday. Use the past simple and begin with “I”.
acceptedAnswers: I met Sofia at a conference yesterday.
speakingExercises.feedback: At a conference identifies the event where the meeting took place.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your friend asks where you spent the evening. Give this fact: I / be / at Daniel’s house / last night. Use the past simple.
acceptedAnswers: I was at Daniel’s house last night.
speakingExercises.feedback: At someone’s house identifies a visit to their home.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct only the preposition in this sentence and speak the whole result: “Their family lives at Edinburgh.”
speakingExercises.feedback: A city treated as a residential area takes in.

speakingExercises.prompt: Compare the transport used by two people in one sentence. Facts: Naomi / travel / on a train; Amir / travel / in a taxi. Use the past simple, start with “Naomi”, and join with “while”.
acceptedAnswers: Naomi travelled on a train while Amir travelled in a taxi.
speakingExercises.feedback: Train takes on and taxi takes in. Both travellers are described in the past.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences. First: the talk / be / at the town hall. Second: the audience / be / in the main room. Use the past simple with “was” for both.
acceptedAnswers: The talk was at the town hall. The audience was in the main room.
speakingExercises.feedback: At gives the venue; in gives the room inside the venue.

speakingExercises.prompt: Someone asks how you rode to the farm. Respond with one full sentence: I / go / on my bike. Use the past simple and start with “I”.
speakingExercises.feedback: The conventional expression is on my bike.

listeningExercises.audioText: Maya was at a wedding on Saturday, but her brother was working at a bakery across town.
listeningExercises.feedback: Maya attended a wedding; her brother was the person at work.

listeningExercises.audioText: I lived in Florence for six months. On the journey home, our train stopped at Pisa for ten minutes.
listeningExercises.prompt: Which city was a brief stop during the journey?
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker lived in Florence, while the train stopped at Pisa.

listeningExercises.audioText: Sonia is waiting at the airport with a sign for the visiting researchers.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word location phrase immediately after “waiting”.
listeningExercises.feedback: At the airport names the place where Sonia is waiting.

listeningExercises.audioText: Our flight was cancelled, so we stayed at the terminal and later went home in a taxi.
listeningExercises.prompt: How did the travellers get home?
listeningExercises.feedback: The audio says they went home in a taxi after the flight was cancelled.

listeningExercises.audioText: The lecture took place at the museum, but the refreshments were served in the courtyard behind it.
listeningExercises.feedback: The museum was the lecture venue, but the refreshments were in the courtyard.

listeningExercises.audioText: The orchestra played at a charity concert, and afterwards the musicians were interviewed in a small dressing room.
listeningExercises.prompt: Where did the interviews take place?
listeningExercises.feedback: The interviews followed the concert and took place in a dressing room.

listeningExercises.audioText: We had to stand on the train because every seat was taken.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word transport phrase immediately after “stand”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Passengers aboard a train are on the train.

listeningExercises.audioText: The visitors went to the hotel in a taxi after their meeting.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word transport phrase immediately after “hotel”.
listeningExercises.feedback: The visitors rode inside a taxi.
